With the amount of time waiting in traffic on the highways and streets of America four years feels like a lifetime. Hell, that thirty seconds waiting behind the asshole who has n't realized the light is green because responding to the text on is phone is a matter of life and death might as well be an eternity. It is n't life that's the Highway, it's the Highway that is life. Just like how people live their lives these days, everyone is in far too much of a rush to pay attention to what's passing them by, even if it costs them. My parents loved to travel when I was a kid, taking the entire family out on long cross-country road trips. Sometimes my brother and I forgot that we even had a home to go back to in the first place. The road was our home. Because of this I developed a knack for spotting all sorts of things. One time on a trip to Yellowstone I was able to count the license plates of forty-nine states. My brother found only ten, neither of us could find Rhode Island. I was the best at the Alphabet Game though. Despite my brother's constant protests that I was a liar, I had a knack for being able to spot any letter even before I could see it.'' I guess you could call it a superpower of mine. My dad loved using my superpower'' for spotting police cars and speed traps, which saved our family thousands in tickets. That was nearly five lifetimes ago, and my wife and I are expecting our second child, a girl. I ca n't wait until both are old enough to play the games I did. While I wait for that, I just spend my time driving to and from work, never the same route twice except for the one major highway. To get anywhere throughout the city you have to drive on the highway which means running into traffic, which means getting angry, which means getting impatient, which means speeding while weaving in and out of traffic.

The room was silent. Tension traveled through the auditorium, dancing with the cigarette smoke that rose from the rows of workstations. John Crawford sat in the back of the auditorium behind the Flight Controller ' s desk. Avoiding the watchful eyes, he grabbed a brush from desk drawer, and began cleaning out his pipe. Something's wrong. " Why isn ' t he saying anything, God damnit?! The procedure was suppose to start five minutes ago! " John twisted the pipe around in his mouth, a habitual act of annoyance. " He said he was grabbing a snack. Keep in mind sir, this is a long and demanding procedure. We want him to be as alert as possible. " Flight Surgeons always put the safety of the astronaut over the mission objective, and John always felt that they were over-cautious. The astronaut was a veteran of the space program. That ' s why he was picked for this mission. Surely someone like Butler can execute this mission without being babied. An hour earlier, Mission Control had been quite a bit louder. John was on his way to winning a hundred dollars from his longtime friend and colleague Bruce Thompson, the Flight Surgeon on duty. John had always been a fan of the Packers, admiring the leadership of Vince Lombardi that he tried to emulate at Mission Control. John was annoyed to learn that the procedure would happen during the Super Bowl, and had requested the game be projected onto the large screen in the front of the auditorium. " I ' ll tell ya, Bruce, Bart Starr has a fire under his ass tonight, and believe me, I ' m as surprised as you are. " Unlike his admiration for Lombardi, John was not a fan of Starr, mostly because Starr consistently beat his alma mater while at Alabama. " I don ' t know, Crawford, I ' ve got a good feeling about the Chiefs Tonight. " Bruce always had a feeling about something, and the smart money always bet against his feelings. John squinted across the hazy room to check the clock. The procedure was suppose to take place at 9:00 pm. Glancing back at the game, he figured he ' d be a hundred dollars richer before it was time to get to work.

He took everything from me. They say revenge is a dish best served cold but I beg to differ. The fear in his eyes, his cold, sweaty hand on my arms. My hand pressed firmly against his throat. He struggled and squirmed but that was too easy. I released my grip, he was panting for air, gasping it for dear life. I never broke contact with his eyes. I saw fear and he saw death. The fire rising in me. I would hurt him like he hurt me. I dug my thumb deep into his eye socket. I felt the squish and pops as I dug deeper. His shrieks echoed through the warehouse. Screams no one would here except me. Screams that would haunt me for the rest of my life. Constantly reminding me what I have done but I was oddly okay about it. I was knuckle deep in his eye when I pulled out. The blood spraying at me. A pool of crimson formed around us. His ungodly scream startled me for a second. Now it was time to end this. I reached for my coat and pulled out a small picture. He knew exactly who they were. He was responsible for their death. It's always the innocents that get killed. The intoxicated drivers always survive. But not always, for today I am death. And I am here for him. My hands wrapped around his throat for one last time. I could feel the life slipping from him. He did n't struggle. He laid limp staring at me. Begging for mercy, he almost looked sorry. But that was to late. My family may of looked sorry and look where they are now. I have become judge, jury, and executioner. His body fell imp on the ground. His life drained. I stood there looking at what I have done. A calming feeling overcame me. I felt relieved. I turned away and walked back towards my car, ready to redo my life once again.

The world here passes me by. Times come and go, but this room never changes. The radio never changes. The recliner I sit in has been here forever and it will be here forever. Time passes here, but it never stays. They call me Lucifer to spite me. They mock me, ignoring my existence as I sit here watching out the window of the damned. They mock me in my own personal hell. Lucifer, the real one, was an old man when I had come. He took to me kindly and I would visit him often after I had died. It was a nice respite from the back-breaking work outside. We would listen to his radio and he would tell me of his life, his faded hopes and dreams. He was a nice man, Lucifer. But he was the Devil. The day he had planned carefully. I walked in and the shades were drawn over the window. A red glow burned through the shades and our shadows were long, undefined. We had tea and he played the music of the angels on the radio. I remember thinking how beautiful it was, hating myself every second for being here and not being up there with them. But Lucifer did not pay attention. He was old and prone to babbling. He babbled plenty that day and he cried often. He cried when he spoke of the early days of Creation. He cried for his youth. I listened as best as I could, but I was n't really paying attention. I listened to the radio, trying to absorb every note instead. And so I had taken the bait. I made the tea, not looking at what I was doing. I focused only on the music and vaguely on Lucifer's words. I poured the tea that would kill the Devil. I saw him sip it and I remember his smile, a subtle thing that broke the spell of the music. You're a good boy,'' he said. You really do n't belong here.'' And he laughed his old man laugh. I think he had wanted to die for a long time. I do n't know why I was the one he chose, but that was how the dice rolled. They found me and I saw the angels first hand. They were mighty beings, more majestic than their song had let on.

I had n't slept in over two days. It felt like my body was turning on me, I lay on my straw mattress at night and attempted to sleep only to gasp for air and have a coughing fit. The physician was traveling to the village due to the large rise in people getting sick. No one really knew how close the doctor was or if he might have a way to help the sickly but everyone held onto that hope. Everyone but me that is. My father and his father before him had both been farmers. I was raised to be a farmer as well, there never was much say in the matter it was simply tradition. When I eventually had a son of mine own he would be raised to be a farmer and the cycle would continue. It had started when the farm hands had started to get sick. Running high fevers some still attempted to attend to the fields until the black lumps began appearing. I'm only one man, I ca n't possibly care for an entire farm by myself, however I still attempted to do some work. Soon enough I began to feel a hotness on my forehead and it increased in heat as time passed. Morticia Tenebrarum ( so named in her ceremony of acceptance to the Temple of the Dead ) stood in a cold, dark hall, staring at the figures before her. As the mist whirled around her, she shivered, left unprotected even under her thick black woolen robes. She stilled her chattering jaw, pulled back her hood, and spoke in a commanding tone: Turn away! Within these halls lie mysteries too terrible to contemplate! Regardless of what you seek, O invaders, you shall not find it between these walls!'' She stood there, hoping the adventurers would get the message and leave, but her luck did n't hold. The pallid man in robes similar to hers raised his hands and sparked two orbs of white-hot flame, while the solidly built woman next to him drew a sword that must have been no more than a foot shorter than Morticia herself. In the same instant, the slim black man at the back of the group notched an arrow, and stood with it pointed directly at her heart. Morticia smiled, despite the fear boiling inside her. She could n't yet summon any more than five skeletons, but hopefully that would be enough to cover her escape while she alerted another more powerful necromancer. She glanced down at the words marked on her arm -- she had n't yet memorized her incantations, something her mentors often chided her over -- and began to speak. She spoke quickly, hoping to avoid a painful death by the archer's arrow, and noticed mid-spell that he had fired. Panicked, she spoke faster, and in her haste tripped over the last word. She closed her eyes, expecting to feel the arrow in her chest. She did n't. Morticia opened her eyes cautiously. The arrow had simply disappeared. Out of thin air, a fountain of sand now issued between her and the adventurers. Before their eyes it shivered, and then coalesced into a figure. A tall, cloaked apparition stood there, holding carelessly in one hand a scythe. As it turned its head, Morticia saw into its hood. A skull lay beneath, dots like black flame dancing in its eyes. This was not supposed to happen. Alice Green, came a voice into Morticia's head, why have you summoned me?

Alex trudged along the parched earth kicking up wisps of dust as he plodded along. It was still relatively early in the morning, but the heat already was starting to become uncomfortable. His heat suit was one of the last ones to not have a hole in it, but then again after the last few years, he started to have plenty to choose from. Alex had remembered his father telling him stories about the Inuit Indians in Canada in the old days. Back when the men had to go out and hunt for their food, they had to wear thick coats that their women had stitched together from the hide from previous kills for them. Each day seemed to be harder than the last and he did n't know how much longer he and the others could keep holding out. Burrowing into the earth had gained a lot of relief from the heat, and there was still a lot of water left. They were making due with reprocessing the water, and using grow lights to provide sunlight that would n't dry out and burn up the plants. The 3D printers were able to make spare parts fairly easy, but the lack of precious metals to make particular circuits meant that they were using older and bulkier boards. It was still an oasis compared to up top where he was making his little trek. He saw an old yellowed and slightly curled up poster in a window for a Christmas sale. It had a snowman hawking the latest and greatest in electronic for deep going out of business discounts with kids in winter clothes playing in the background. He stopped and stared at the poster and tried to remember the last time he had seen snow. Two decades at least. Maybe three? The only thing that keeps time anymore is death as far as he knew. He thought back to the stories about the Inuit his father had told him and thought how he was in the same boat as they were in some ways. The main difference was that the heat was the culprit and not the cold. Without protection, you would eventually die. The earth was without protection, so it was dying. The layers of protection were like the layers I put on to keep from getting damaged from the heat.

With acid in my stomach and the onset of nausea taking over my usually-reserved faculties, I did my best to take the seat directly across from her, my cup imperceptibly trembling in my hand. I feared this woman, and she knew it.

D-day. Looks like it's the blindfold. It's my last hope. I've always been in control of my future. I'll give that up over my dead body. The plan is pretty simple. I go down to the basement. There's nothing in the basement. I lock and bar the basement from the inside. I put the blindfold on. I sit there for twenty-four hours. The vision of darkness I had three days ago comes into fruition. Not death, just darkness because of the blindfold. It's close to fail-safe. Or at least, it's far more fail-safe than trying to figure out what spells my doom. I do n't understand how ordinary people can live like this, not knowing. The stories they tell themselves, about luck, gods, guardian angels, how could they bet their lives on such ludicrous fantasies? Three hours in. I'm hungry. That's fine, I ca n't starve in twenty-four hours. Maybe I should have brought some snacks, to pass the time at least. No, wait, you thought about this. You could choke. Even though you're a grown man and you know how to chew, something could go wrong and you could die. But then again, this house could collapse. It does happen. Dodgy builders, bad materials. Maybe a freak storm? A hurricane out of nowhere. Maybe a bomb will go off outside? They're always on the lookout for terrorists at important buildings and monuments, so why would n't a smart terrorist target some quiet neighborhood in some insignificant town? Or maybe it'll just be a gas leak. Wait, is that gas? I can smell something. Oh, that's just me. Oh. This is what it is. This is normal. This is why people believe in guardian angels and luck and all the rest of it. The world is a truly frightening place. Nothing would ever get done if people thought about that all the time. And this is what I'm going to have to get used to. I do n't get visions three days into the future anymore. I just see darkness. At first I feared it meant death, but now I see that it's a fate far worse than that. To hell with that. I take off the blindfold. I get up and leave the basement. I take the gun down from where it hangs above my mantle-piece. I remain in control of my own future, to the last moment.

He looked like the kind of guy you would see at an accounting firm or shopping at the mall. You know, short, styled hair, clean suit. Sometimes it hadn ' t even been three days before he showed up again. Other times, it would be weeks. But he always came back. And he always ordered the same thing: a tally mark. What was he counting? The grid of tally marks already stretched a quarter of the way down his back. Was he an underground fighter? He never displayed any obvious injuries. A hitman? He hung up his shirt and jacket and lied face down on the tattoo bed. The last tally was still a little raw from a few days ago. A quick count told me he was up to 124. I silenced my curiosity and began preparing the needle. The man was lying still, silent, and calm.
